hero.title: Why abstract?
intro.0: Why hide logic behind an interface, instead of just using the class you already have? At first the extra step looks like a waste. But the moment you need a second kind of thing, code tied to one class gets in the way. Here you'll see how a shared promise lets one piece of code work with many types - even ones you write later.
task.1.title: Two animals, same shape
task.1.context: A cat and a dog both make a sound, each in its own way. Write both classes from scratch: a `Cat` whose `Speak()` returns `"Meow"`, and a `Dog` whose `Speak()` returns `"Woof"`. They do the same kind of job - but nothing in the code links them yet.
task.1.goal.0: Write a `Cat` class and a `Dog` class, each with a `Speak()` method.
task.1.goal.1: Cat says Meow, Dog says Woof. Main prints both, so the output is two lines: Meow then Woof.
task.2.title: A keeper stuck on one animal
task.2.context: Write a `Keeper` with a method `Greet(Cat cat)` that returns `"heard: "` followed by what the cat says. Because it is typed to `Cat`, a dog will never fit it - even though a dog can speak too. That is the cost of tying a method to one class; the next task removes it.
task.2.goal.0: Write a `Keeper` class with a method `Greet(Cat cat)` that returns `"heard: "` plus `cat.Speak()`.
task.2.goal.1: Main greets a cat, so the output is heard: Meow.
task.3.title: Name the promise
task.3.context: An interface is the shared shape written down: a promise that says `Speak()` exists, without saying what the sound is. Write an `IAnimal` interface with a `Speak()` method, then write `Cat` and `Dog` that keep that promise with `: IAnimal`.
task.3.goal.1: Write `Cat : IAnimal` (says Meow) and `Dog : IAnimal` (says Woof).
task.3.goal.2: Main holds a Dog in an `IAnimal` and speaks, so the output is Woof.
task.4.title: Depend on the promise, not the animal
task.4.context: Now write a `Keeper` whose `Greet` takes an `IAnimal` instead of a `Cat`. That one change is all it takes: the same method now greets a cat, a dog, or anything else that keeps the promise.
task.4.goal.0: Write a `Keeper` with `Greet(IAnimal animal)` returning `"heard: "` plus `animal.Speak()`.
task.4.goal.1: Main greets a Dog through it, so the output is heard: Woof.
task.5.title: A new animal walks in for free
task.5.context: Because `Greet` depends on `IAnimal`, you can add a brand-new animal without touching the keeper. The `Keeper` below is finished. Write a new `Owl` class that keeps the `IAnimal` promise and says `"Hoot"`, and it walks straight through the unchanged method.
task.5.goal.1: Main runs the unchanged `Greet` with an Owl, so the output is heard: Hoot.
task.6.title: Why abstract? - recap
task.6.context: An interface is a promise written down. Keep the promise, and your code fits anywhere.
task.6.summaryIntro: Pulling logic behind an interface lets one piece of code work with many different types, now and later.
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: A shared shape -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: two classes can do the same kind of job in their own way.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: interface -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: writes that shared promise down: the method exists, without the how.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: `: IAnimal` -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: a class declares it keeps the promise.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: Program to the interface -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: depend on the promise, so any keeper of it fits.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: Open to new types -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: a brand-new class drops in without touching the caller.
concept.pr-interface.def: A named promise of what methods a type offers, without saying how they work.
concept.pr-program-to-interface.def: Depending on the promise rather than a concrete type, so any type that keeps it can be used.
task.6.summaryItems.5.title: In SOLID -
task.6.summaryItems.5.text: a new type dropping in without editing the caller is the **O**, Open/Closed; depending on the promise is the abstraction the **D** (Dependency Inversion) later builds on.
